legions.name: Ioviani (seniores and iuniores)
legions.endNote: Ioviani seniores in the West (Not. Occ. 5), Ioviani iuniores in the East (Not. Or. 5)

stations.note: Illyrian origin; the Martiobarbuli of Vegetius

legions.summary: Senior palatine legion of the late army, named after Diocletian's divine patron Jupiter. Vegetius says two Illyrian legions of 6,000 men, expert with lead-weighted darts (mattiobarbuli), were renamed Ioviani and Herculiani by Diocletian and Maximian (1.17).
legions.detail: The Ioviani acclaimed Jovian emperor in 363 after Julian's death, since Jovian's father had been their commander (Amm. 25.5.8). With the division of 364 the unit split into seniores (West) and iuniores (East). Its shield pattern is drawn in the Notitia.

legions.name: Herculiani (seniores and iuniores)
legions.endNote: Herculiani seniores in the West, iuniores in the East (Notitia)
legions.summary: Twin of the Ioviani, named for Maximian's patron Hercules. The two units headed the precedence of the palatine legions in both halves of the empire.
legions.detail: Ammianus mentions the Ioviani and Herculiani in Julian's Persian campaign (363), where they fought in the rearguard (25.6.3). Maximian's Herculian ideology (Herculius as his signum) is mirrored in the unit's name.

legions.name: Lanciarii seniores

stations.note: tetrarchic comitatus; tombstones at Apamea and in the Balkans

legions.summary: Javelin-armed elite unit of the tetrarchic comitatus, recorded as lanciarii on Diocletianic tombstones and later as a senior palatine legion of the East.
legions.detail: The Lanciarii and Mattiarii formed the strong core of Valens's army at Adrianople (378) and were overwhelmed when the reserve Batavi failed to come up (Amm. 31.13.8).

legions.name: Lanciarii Sabarienses
legions.summary: Western palatine legion named after Savaria (Szombathely) in Pannonia, one of several late units whose names derive from their original garrison towns.

legions.name: Mattiarii (seniores and iuniores)
legions.summary: Palatine legion armed with lead-weighted darts (mattiobarbuli or plumbatae, from mattea, a mace). It fought in the line at Adrianople, where its commander and many men fell.

legions.name: Divitenses (seniores)

stations.note: Divitia (Köln-Deutz), bridgehead fort built by Constantine c. 310

legions.summary: Named after the Constantinian bridgehead fort of Divitia opposite Cologne, built c. 310, from which the core of II Italica's or XXII Primigenia's detachments was drawn.

legions.name: Tungrecani (seniores)
legions.summary: Late palatine legion paired with the Divitenses, named after the Tungri of Germania Secunda. In 365 the two units went over to the usurper Procopius at Constantinople.

legions.name: Cornuti (seniores)

stations.note: Constantine's army at the Milvian Bridge (shown on the Arch of Constantine)

legions.summary: 'The Horned Ones', an auxilium palatinum of Germanic recruits whose horned helmets appear on the frieze of the Arch of Constantine. With the Bracchiati they held the right of the line at Strasbourg (357), raising the barritus war-cry.

legions.name: Petulantes
legions.summary: Gallic auxilium palatinum which, with the Celtae, refused Constantius II's order to march east in February 360 and proclaimed Julian Augustus at Lutetia (Paris).
legions.detail: Ammianus (20.4) says the soldiers feared leaving their families exposed to the Alamanni; Julian was raised on a shield and crowned with a neck torque of a standard-bearer.

legions.name: Legio I Iovia Scythica
legions.endNote: listed at Noviodunum in the Notitia
legions.summary: One of the two Diocletianic legions of the new province of Scythia Minor, sharing the name of the emperor's divine patron. Its base at Noviodunum guarded the Danube crossing used by Valens in 369.

legions.name: Legio II Herculia
legions.endNote: listed at Troesmis in the Notitia
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of Scythia Minor at Troesmis, named after Maximian's patron Hercules, pair to I Iovia at Noviodunum.

legions.name: Legio IV Martia
legions.endNote: listed at Betthorus in the Notitia; fortress abandoned after the earthquake of 551 or earlier
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of Arabia at Betthorus (el-Lejjun), a 4.6-hectare fortress excavated by S. T. Parker's Limes Arabicus Project; its smaller size reflects late legions of perhaps 1,000-2,000 men.
legions.detail: The fortress shows a reduction of the barracks in the 5th century and a church built inside; the garrison seems to have been demobilised under Justinian, who relied on Ghassanid allies.

legions.name: Legio I Illyricorum
legions.endNote: listed at Palmyra in the Notitia

stations.note: camp of Diocletian built in the western quarter of the city

legions.summary: Legion probably formed from Illyrian troops after Aurelian's destruction of Palmyra in 273 and stationed in the 'Camp of Diocletian' inside the ruined city on the Strata Diocletiana.

legions.name: Legio I Pontica
legions.endNote: listed at Trapezus in the Notitia
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of the Pontic frontier at Trapezus, guarding the Black Sea end of the road to Satala and Armenia.

legions.name: Legio V Parthica
legions.endNote: destroyed when Shapur II stormed Amida in 359
legions.summary: Garrison legion of Amida on the upper Tigris. In 359 it held Amida for 73 days against Shapur II alongside the Magnentian legions and others; Ammianus Marcellinus, inside the city, escaped and wrote the eyewitness account.

legions.name: Theban Legion (Thebaei)
legions.endNote: Thebaei listed among the western palatine legions; the martyr legion of Agaunum is legendary
legions.summary: Late units called Thebaei appear in the Notitia. The legend of St Maurice and the 6,600 Christian soldiers of the Theban Legion massacred at Agaunum by Maximian is told by Eucherius of Lyon (c. 430-450) and is unhistorical in its numbers and details.
